title: Donald Trump uses Trump Foundation to bribe Florida Attorney General
description_short: Donald Trump uses Trump Foundation to bribe Florida Attorney General
description_medium: A 2016 Washington Post report said the Trump Foundation made a $25,000 contribution in 2013 to a political group connected to Florida Attorney General Pam Bondi while her office was considering Trump University fraud allegations. The Foundation later reported the payment as an illegal political contribution and corrected its filing. The timing does not by itself establish a bribe or agreement.
description_long: The Trump Foundation paid $25,000 in 2013 to a political group connected to Florida Attorney General Pam Bondi, according to reporting summarized in the linked account and a 2016 Washington Post report. Bondi’s office was considering whether to pursue fraud allegations involving Trump University, but later did not take action. The Foundation had reported the payment as a donation to a Kansas charity with a similar name; that charity did not receive the money. Trump later corrected the Foundation’s IRS filing, paid a $2,500 penalty, and reimbursed the Foundation, according to a Trump Organization official. The Foundation acknowledged the payment was an illegal political contribution. These facts establish a prohibited contribution and a close sequence between the donation and Bondi’s decision. They do not establish that Trump paid Bondi personally, that she agreed to a trade, or that the contribution caused her office’s decision. The title’s use of “bribe” asserts an exchange that the supplied record does not prove. A contemporaneous payment date and evidence of an agreement would be needed to support that allegation.
subcategory: Political contribution and attorney general decision

preserved_fields.title: Donald Trump uses Trump Foundation to bribe Florida Attorney General
preserved_fields.description_short: Donald Trump uses Trump Foundation to bribe Florida Attorney General

notes: Missing context: the exact payment date and evidence that Bondi agreed to exchange official action for the contribution. The sources support an illegal political donation, timing and later correction, not a proven quid pro quo. Proposed correction: use “illegal political contribution” unless evidence establishes bribery.

title: Donald Trump gives out Sen. Lindsey Graham's personal cell number
description_short: Donald Trump gives out Sen. Lindsey Graham's personal cell number
description_medium: At a campaign appearance on July 21, 2015, Trump displayed and read aloud Senator Lindsey Graham’s personal phone number. Graham had criticized Trump’s candidacy and later said he changed his phone number. The linked account presents the disclosure as part of their public political dispute; it does not report a criminal case or physical injury resulting from the incident.
description_long: During a campaign appearance on July 21, 2015, Donald Trump held up a piece of paper with Senator Lindsey Graham’s personal phone number and read it aloud to the crowd and cameras. The linked account places the disclosure amid a dispute over Trump’s presidential candidacy after Graham criticized him. It says Graham subsequently changed his phone and number. Graham continued to criticize Trump after the event, including questioning his readiness to handle military and foreign-policy matters, so the exposure did not end their political disagreement. The immediate consequence described is the disruption of Graham’s contact arrangements. The supplied account does not document a resulting physical injury, a criminal charge or a court ruling about this specific incident. Publishing private contact details can expose a person to unwanted calls and messages, but the record does not quantify what Graham received. The incident is best described as a public disclosure of a senator’s personal phone number during a campaign dispute, with a reported change of number afterward.

preserved_fields.title: Donald Trump gives out Sen. Lindsey Graham's personal cell number
preserved_fields.description_short: Donald Trump gives out Sen. Lindsey Graham's personal cell number

notes: The source describes a disclosure and subsequent number change. Its general legal commentary is not a court finding about this incident.

title: CDC and NIH Biomedical Research Destruction - $18 Billion Federal Science Elimination
description_short: CDC and NIH Biomedical Research Destruction - $18 Billion Federal Science Elimination
description_medium: Nature reported that NIH had terminated nearly 800 research projects by April 2025. A separate Science report described a proposed FY2026 NIH budget reduction to $26.7 billion and a reorganization requiring congressional approval. The supplied sources do not establish an enacted $18 billion cut, the final NIH appropriation or specific effects on CDC programs.
description_long: The linked reporting documents concerns about federal biomedical research funding, but it does not support the title’s claim that $18 billion in NIH and CDC research was eliminated on January 20, 2025. Nature reported that NIH had terminated nearly 800 research projects by April 2025. STAT described instability reported by researchers whose grants were disrupted. A separate Science article covered an administration proposal to reduce the NIH budget to $26.7 billion in FY2026 and reorganize the agency; the article notes that Congress would need to approve the proposal. A proposed budget is not an enacted appropriation, and the project count does not establish a final dollar reduction or prove that all affected awards were cancelled permanently. The supplied material also does not identify which CDC chronic-disease programs ended, when changes took effect or what services were affected. These sources support reporting on project terminations and a proposed budget change, not the title’s broad claim of a completed $18 billion elimination across NIH and CDC. Enacted funding records and program-level cancellation notices are needed to describe the total and consequences accurately.
organization_tags: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

preserved_fields.title: CDC and NIH Biomedical Research Destruction - $18 Billion Federal Science Elimination
preserved_fields.description_short: CDC and NIH Biomedical Research Destruction - $18 Billion Federal Science Elimination

notes: Missing context: enacted NIH and CDC appropriations, project-level termination records, the actual funding change, and the specific CDC programs affected. The packet gives a project count and a proposed NIH budget, not an enacted $18 billion cut. Proposed correction: describe terminations and the FY2026 proposal separately until final funding and CDC effects are documented.

title: Donald Trump Jr. is paid $50,000 to meet with Russian assets in Paris
description_short: Donald Trump Jr. is paid $50,000 to meet with Russian assets in Paris
description_medium: A Trump File account says Donald Trump Jr. received at least $50,000 to attend a private event in Paris hosted by the Center for Political and Foreign Affairs. It describes the group as a Russian influence operation and reports that organizer Randa Kassis later discussed the meeting with Russian officials. The supplied record does not independently establish the payment or that attendees were intelligence assets.
description_long: According to the linked account, Donald Trump Jr. attended a private event of about 30 people at the Ritz Hotel in Paris in October 2016 and received at least $50,000. The event was hosted by the Center for Political and Foreign Affairs, whose organizers Fabien Baussart and Randa Kassis were described as having ties to Russian officials. Kassis said she later discussed the dinner with Mikhail Bogdanov, a Russian deputy foreign minister, and wrote that she hoped Trump’s election would enable U.S.–Russia cooperation over Syria. She also said she had conveyed an idea for cooperation through Trump Jr. These statements document what the organizer claimed about the meeting and its follow-up; they do not establish that Trump Jr. passed a policy proposal to his father or that any agreement resulted. The supplied page calls the event’s hosts Russian intelligence assets and attributes an assessment to French intelligence, but does not include the underlying assessment or payment documentation. The headline’s description of participants as “Russian assets” therefore needs independent corroboration. The reported paid appearance and post-election contacts can be described with attribution, while the payment terms and intelligence characterization remain unverified here.
topic_tags: Center for Political and Foreign Affairs
organization_tags: Center for Political and Foreign Affairs

preserved_fields.title: Donald Trump Jr. is paid $50,000 to meet with Russian assets in Paris
preserved_fields.description_short: Donald Trump Jr. is paid $50,000 to meet with Russian assets in Paris

notes: Missing context: independent evidence for the $50,000 payment and French intelligence assessment, plus corroboration of what was conveyed and to whom. The linked page attributes the intelligence characterization and follow-up claims but does not provide the underlying records. Proposed correction: describe a reported paid appearance and attributed Russian contacts rather than calling participants intelligence assets without supporting evidence.

title: Trump: State Dept. blocks autopsy results of Trump-Russia figure Vitaly Churkin
description_short: Trump: State Dept. blocks autopsy results of Trump-Russia figure Vitaly Churkin
description_medium: Vitaly Churkin, Russia’s U.N. ambassador, died in New York on February 20, 2017. The city medical examiner initially said toxicology was needed before determining the cause, then did not release the autopsy results. A linked account alleges federal officials and Russia pressed the city to withhold them, but the supplied material does not independently document that pressure or connect Trump to the decision.
description_long: Vitaly Churkin, Russia’s ambassador to the United Nations, died in New York on February 20, 2017. The linked timeline says the city medical examiner’s office initially could not determine the cause without toxicology and later declined to release the autopsy results. It alleges that federal officials lobbied New York City to withhold the findings and direct inquiries to the State Department, citing a claimed legal obligation to respect Churkin and Russia’s objection to disclosure. The account does not include the officials’ letters or other independent records of the lobbying, so the extent and authority of any federal pressure remain unverified. It also notes that Churkin met Donald Trump at a 1986 luncheon and later defended him at United Nations meetings. Those earlier contacts do not show that Trump influenced the medical examiner’s decision. The available description does not establish why the results were withheld, what legal rule controlled disclosure or whether the State Department blocked release. The reported death and initial toxicology delay can be stated, but the alleged pressure and Trump connection require supporting documents before the title’s claim is treated as fact.
subcategory: Autopsy disclosure and alleged federal pressure
organization_tags: New York City Office of Chief Medical Examiner

preserved_fields.title: Trump: State Dept. blocks autopsy results of Trump-Russia figure Vitaly Churkin
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: State Dept. blocks autopsy results of Trump-Russia figure Vitaly Churkin

notes: Missing context: city or federal records showing who requested withholding, under what legal authority and whether State Department officials directed the decision. The linked page alleges pressure but supplies no independent documentation. Proposed correction: describe the non-release and its stated reasons separately from the unverified pressure claim.

title: Trump: Epstein consults Ken Starr to protect Trump
description_short: Trump: Epstein consults Ken Starr to protect Trump
description_medium: Trump File reports that Jeffrey Epstein emailed on August 23, 2018, saying he had spoken with attorney Ken Starr the day before, when Michael Cohen pleaded guilty to campaign-finance violations tied to Trump. Starr later joined Trump’s Senate impeachment defense. The linked page does not provide the full email or show that advice reached Trump.
description_long: Michael Cohen pleaded guilty on August 22, 2018, to campaign-finance violations connected to payments for the Trump campaign. Trump File reports that Jeffrey Epstein sent an email the next day saying he had spoken with attorney Ken Starr the previous day. The account presents the conversation as legal strategy that could help Trump avoid consequences and notes that Starr later joined Trump’s Senate impeachment defense in January 2020. The chronology connects Epstein’s reported conversation with Starr to Cohen’s plea and Starr’s later role, but it does not establish what they discussed. The page does not reproduce the complete email thread, identify every sender and recipient or show that Trump was part of the conversation. It also does not demonstrate that Starr gave advice to Trump, that Epstein transmitted advice to him or that any strategy changed a legal outcome. The event can be described as a reported conversation between Epstein and Starr, followed by Starr’s later participation in Trump’s defense. The title’s claim that Epstein consulted Starr to protect Trump goes beyond what the available email summary establishes.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Epstein consults Ken Starr to protect Trump
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Epstein consults Ken Starr to protect Trump

notes: Missing context: the complete email exchange, full sender and recipient list, the subjects discussed and evidence that advice reached Trump or affected his defense. Proposed correction: title as a reported Epstein–Starr conversation unless further records establish its purpose.

title: Trump tells China's president he approves of Muslim concentration camps
description_short: Trump tells China's president he approves of Muslim concentration camps
description_medium: John Bolton’s account says Trump told Xi Jinping in June 2019 that he approved of China’s detention camps for Uyghurs and other Muslim minorities. Bolton’s recollection is the supplied basis for the private exchange; the packet does not provide a transcript or independent corroboration. The account also refers to an earlier similar conversation recalled by Matthew Pottinger.
description_long: The linked account attributes to former national security adviser John Bolton a private conversation between Donald Trump and Chinese president Xi Jinping at the opening dinner of the June 2019 G20 summit in Osaka. Bolton later wrote that Trump expressed approval of China’s detention camps for Muslim minorities in Xinjiang while Xi explained the policy. The account also refers to Matthew Pottinger’s recollection of a similar exchange in 2017. These are retrospective descriptions of private remarks, not a public transcript or an official finding. The supplied material does not establish the exact wording, whether Trump used the term “concentration camps,” or the full context of the conversation. It also does not show what policy decisions followed from the reported remarks. The episode, if accurately recalled, would concern a president’s response to China’s detention policy in a private diplomatic discussion. The details should remain attributed to Bolton and Pottinger until corroborated by contemporaneous records or other participants. The title states both the wording and approval as fact, while the available account supports an attributed recollection that needs careful qualification.
subcategory: Reported discussion of Xinjiang detention camps

preserved_fields.title: Trump tells China's president he approves of Muslim concentration camps
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump tells China's president he approves of Muslim concentration camps

notes: Missing context: no transcript or contemporaneous record of the private exchange; the supplied account largely reproduces Bolton’s retrospective recollection and references Pottinger’s account of a similar earlier remark. Needed: exact wording and corroboration. Proposed correction: attribute the claim to Bolton rather than present it as independently verified.

title: Trump Admin buys 3.5 million contaminated COVID-19 tests from Abu Dhabi
description_short: Trump Admin buys 3.5 million contaminated COVID-19 tests from Abu Dhabi
description_medium: A shipment of 3.5 million Chinese-made coronavirus tests arrived in Washington from Abu Dhabi on March 31, 2020, after a White House purchase, according to the linked account. It cites government laboratory tests finding the kits contaminated and unusable; some were distributed by FEMA to states. The reporting could not identify who authorized the purchase.
description_long: The linked account says a shipment of 3.5 million Chinese-made COVID-19 tests arrived in Washington, D.C., from Abu Dhabi on March 31, 2020, after a White House purchase. It cites documents obtained by Vanity Fair that showed two government laboratories found the tests “contaminated and unusable.” Some of the tests had already been distributed by FEMA to states, so the shipment did not provide the testing support expected from the order. The investigators cited in the report could not identify who made the purchase, which the timeline describes as unauthorized. The same account says Jared Kushner was leading a task force to expand testing and that the effort was later abandoned, but it does not show that he ordered the shipment. The report documents a large procurement with serious quality-control and accountability questions during the early COVID-19 response. It does not identify the responsible buyer or explain how many kits reached states before the laboratory findings. The account supports the contamination claim through government test results, while responsibility for the procurement remains unresolved.

preserved_fields.title: Trump Admin buys 3.5 million contaminated COVID-19 tests from Abu Dhabi
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump Admin buys 3.5 million contaminated COVID-19 tests from Abu Dhabi

notes: The linked account attributes the laboratory findings to documents obtained by Vanity Fair. It does not identify who authorized the purchase; the task-force connection does not establish Jared Kushner ordered it.
